accuracy.evidence: Checked against CCSS 5.NF.B.4b (tile a rectangle with unit-fraction squares; area equals the product of the side lengths) and the National Curriculum for England Year 6 (multiply simple pairs of proper fractions, writing the answer in its simplest form). Every lab product recomputed: 1/2 × 1/3 = 1/6, 2/5 × 3/4 = 6/20, 2/3 × 4/5 = 8/15, 3/4 × 2/3 = 6/12 = 1/2, 3/2 × 2/3 = 6/6 = 1, 3/5 × 1/2 = 3/10, 1/4 × 1/2 = 1/8. The topic's own evidence example (2/3 × 3/4 tiled with 1/12 squares = 6/12 = 1/2) is the core build step. Parameterised answers a, 2c and a·c are whole numbers at every corner of their ranges, each with at least 4 distinct values.

misconceptions.evidence: Distractors come from the documented errors in the adult notes: adding tops and bottoms (5/7, 3/7, 4/6), adding denominators for the tile size (1/7 instead of 1/12), multiplication always makes bigger, counting against the whole two-square drawing (3/6 instead of 6/6) and splitting a mixed number. The wrong-path script clicked them: 'You added: 1+1 over 2+3. Count the tiles: 1 shaded, and one square holds 2 × 3 = 6 tiles' and 'B is shaded the full height, so it shows 3/5 × 1, not × 1/2'.

lab_distinct.evidence: gate_lab_distinct passed under the 30% shingle limit. No other lab cuts a unit square into b × d unit-fraction tiles and drags a snapping corner to build a fractional rectangle, then extends past 1 with two unit squares. flagtiles (Area by Tiling) uses whole unit squares, and lesson 867 multiplies a fraction by a whole number on a number line, not as an area.

lab_teaches.evidence: Six steps build the rule: cut the square into twelfths and see that 3 × 4 gives the tile size; drag to 3/4 × 2/3 and count 6 of 12; three more products where shaded tiles go on top and tiles per square on the bottom; a side longer than 1 (1 1/2 × 2/3 = 1); matching squares to products; then the challenge. Each step ends with a stated rule.

predictions.evidence: Three locked-in predictions: the tile size for thirds × quarters (1/12 vs 1/7 vs 1/4), whether 3/4 × 2/3 is smaller than 3/4, and 1 1/2 × 2/3 (1 vs 1 2/3 vs 2/6). Each tempting option is disproved by the lab's own count, and the reveal repeats the learner's choice.

challenge_feedback.evidence: The Challenge cycles six questions (a product, bigger or smaller, a rug in m², tile size, a mixed number, counting 1/20 tiles) with rotated answer order. Each wrong tag has its own message, e.g. '5 strips one way and 2 the other make 5 × 2 = 10 tiles, not 5 + 2' and '1 1/2 is 3/2. 3/2 × 1/2 = 3/4'.

readability.evidence: Kid explanation FK grade 1.6 overall (0.3, 2.5, 1.5, 2.8), under the 6.5 limit. Adult notes FK 5.5, under 9.5, after the long mistakes sentence was split. Numerator and denominator are said as tops and bottoms for the learner and named properly for adults.

no_filler.evidence: gate_content passed with overlap under 12%. Every kid paragraph carries a fact the items test (12 tiles, 6/12 = 1/2, not 5/7, 1 1/2 × 2/3 = 1). Adult notes give the two curriculum statements, the general ac/bd argument and the named mistakes.

mobile.evidence: Screenshot QA at 360 × 640 in light and dark found the cut chips and the area options hidden behind the feedback box; on phones the cut chips now sit side by side under the grid, the area choices are HTML buttons only, the info box folds to two lines and the grid is capped at 34% of the canvas height. The corner handle is a 44 px target and Wider, Narrower, Taller and Shorter buttons do the same job.

accessibility.evidence: gate_browser runs axe WCAG 2.1 AA in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13, every Show me finishes with a tick, and the screenshot runs had no console or page errors. The canvas sits on a light card in dark mode with a live aria-label (e.g. 'Rectangle 3/4 wide and 2/3 tall: 6 tiles, each 1/12 of a square'), and every canvas action has a button.
